q: When did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?

August 1920
March 1930
April 1919

q: Who wrote the famous book "Hind Swaraj" in 1909?
o: Jawaharlal Nehru
Mahatma Gandhi
Subhas Chandra Bose
Sardar Patel
e: In his famous book Hind Swaraj (1909), Mahatma Gandhi declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and survived only because of it.

q: In which city did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place on 13 April 1919?
o: Lahore
Amritsar
Delhi
Lucknow
e: The infamous Jallianwala Bagh incident took place on 13 April 1919 in Amritsar, where General Dyer opened fire on a large unarmed crowd gathered on Baisakhi.

q: In which year did Mahatma Gandhi travel to Champaran in Bihar to inspire peasants against the oppressive plantation system?
e: In 1917, Mahatma Gandhi travelled to Champaran in Bihar to inspire the peasants to struggle against the oppressive indigo plantation system.

q: Which Act of 1919 gave the British government enormous powers to repress political activities and detain political prisoners without trial for two years?
o: Government of India Act
Rowlatt Act
Inland Emigration Act
Vernacular Press Act
e: The Rowlatt Act (1919) was hurriedly passed through the Imperial Legislative Council despite united opposition from Indian members, allowing detention without trial for two years.

q: Who led the peasant movement in Awadh during the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: Alluri Sitaram Raju
Baba Ramchandra
C. R. Das
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
e: In Awadh, peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra — a sanyasi who had earlier been to Fiji as an indentured labourer — against talukdars and landlords.

q: Who led the militant guerrilla movement in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Baba Ramchandra
Alluri Sitaram Raju
Abdul Ghaffar Khan
Chittaranjan Das
e: In the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh, a militant guerrilla movement spread in the early 1920s led by Alluri Sitaram Raju.

q: At which session of the Indian National Congress was the resolution of "Purna Swaraj" (complete independence) formalised in December 1929?
o: Nagpur Session
Calcutta Session
Lahore Session
Madras Session
e: In December 1929, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, the Lahore Congress formalised the demand of "Purna Swaraj" or full independence for India.

q: Which date was declared to be celebrated as Independence Day during the Lahore Congress session of 1929?
o: 15 August 1930
26 January 1930
13 April 1930
12 March 1930
e: The Lahore Congress declared that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day when people were to take a pledge to struggle for complete independence.

q: Who formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics?
o: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru
Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Patel
Maulana Azad and Shaukat Ali
e: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics and oppose British policies within councils.

q: Who was known as "Frontier Gandhi" (सीमांत गांधी)?
o: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
Abdul Ghaffar Khan
Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
Shaukat Ali
e: Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a devout disciple of Mahatma Gandhi from the North-West Frontier Province, was arrested in April 1930 during the Civil Disobedience Movement.

q: Between whom was the Poona Pact of September 1932 signed?
o: Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin
Mahatma Gandhi and Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Jawaharlal Nehru and Muhammad Ali Jinnah
Subhas Chandra Bose and C. R. Das
e: Dr B. R. Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhiji's position and the result was the Poona Pact of September 1932, granting reserved seats for Depressed Classes within the general electorate.

q: Who wrote the hymn "Vande Mataram" in the 1870s and later included it in the novel "Anandamath"?
o: Rabindranath Tagore
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
Abanindranath Tagore
Natesa Sastri
e: In the 1870s, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote "Vande Mataram" as a hymn to the motherland and later included it in his novel Anandamath.

q: Who painted the famous image of Bharat Mata in 1905 depicting her as an ascetic figure?
o: Raja Ravi Varma
Abanindranath Tagore
Nandalal Bose
Jamini Roy
e: Moved by the Swadeshi movement, Abanindranath Tagore painted his famous image of Bharat Mata (1905) portraying her as an ascetic figure — calm, composed, divine and spiritual.

q: Which incident in February 1922 led Mahatma Gandhi to call off the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: Jallianwala Bagh massacre
Chauri Chaura incident
Signing of Poona Pact
Arrival of Simon Commission
e: At Chauri Chaura in Gorakhpur (February 1922), a peaceful demonstration in a bazaar turned into a violent clash with the police; hearing of it, Gandhi halted the Non-Cooperation Movement.

q: Who organised the Dalits into the "Depressed Classes Association" in 1930?
o: Mahatma Gandhi
Dr B. R. Ambedkar
Jyotiba Phule
Periyar E. V. Ramasamy
e: Dr B. R. Ambedkar organised the dalits into the Depressed Classes Association in 1930 and demanded separate electorates for them at the Second Round Table Conference.

q: When did the Dandi March (Salt March) begin from Sabarmati Ashram?
o: 26 January 1930
12 March 1930
6 April 1930
5 March 1931
e: Mahatma Gandhi started his famous salt march on 12 March 1930 accompanied by 78 of his trusted volunteers from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi.

q: On which date did Mahatma Gandhi reach Dandi and ceremonially violate the salt law?
o: 12 March 1930
6 April 1930
13 April 1930
5 March 1931
e: On 6 April 1930, Mahatma Gandhi reached the coastal town of Dandi after walking 240 miles over 24 days and manufactured salt by boiling sea water.

q: When was the Quit India Resolution passed by the All India Congress Committee in Bombay?
o: 8 August 1942
15 August 1942
26 January 1942
14 July 1942
e: On 8 August 1942 in Bombay, the All India Congress Committee endorsed the Quit India resolution, where Gandhiji delivered the famous "Do or Die" speech.

q: Who formed the Khilafat Committee in Bombay in March 1919?
o: Jinnah and Liaquat Ali
Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali
Abdul Ghaffar Khan and Hakim Ajmal Khan
Syed Ahmad Khan and Maulana Azad
e: To defend the Ottoman Khalifa's temporal powers after WWI, a Khilafat Committee was formed in Bombay in March 1919 by young Muslim leaders Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali.

q: In which year was the Non-Cooperation Movement programme formally adopted at the Nagpur Congress session?
o: September 1920
December 1920
January 1921
February 1922
e: After initial reluctance within Congress, at the Nagpur session in December 1920 a compromise was worked out and the Non-Cooperation programme was adopted.

q: When did the Simon Commission arrive in India?
e: When the all-British Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928, it was greeted with the slogan "Go back Simon" because it had not a single Indian member.

q: What was "begar" (बेगार) that peasants in Awadh protested against?
o: A fixed annual harvest tax paid to the British crown
Labour that villagers were forced to contribute without any payment
A religious pilgrimage tax
Forced military service overseas
e: Begar means labour that villagers were forced to contribute at landlords' farms without any payment.

q: In 1921, Mahatma Gandhi designed the Swaraj flag. Which colours were in it and what was at its centre?
o: Red, green and white; a spinning wheel (charkha)
Red, green and yellow; eight lotuses
Saffron, white and blue; a lion
Orange and green; a plough
e: By 1921, Gandhiji had designed the Swaraj flag: a tricolour (red, green and white) with a spinning wheel in the centre representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help.

q: Who published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales titled "The Folklore of Southern India"?
o: Rabindranath Tagore
Natesa Sastri
Subramania Bharati
Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
e: In Madras, Natesa Sastri published a massive four-volume collection of Tamil folk tales, The Folklore of Southern India, believing folklore was national literature.

q: When was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed?
o: 5 March 1931
12 March 1930
26 January 1930
24 September 1932
e: On 5 March 1931, Mahatma Gandhi entered into a pact with Viceroy Irwin, agreeing to participate in the Second Round Table Conference in London while the government agreed to release political prisoners.

q: In 1918, Mahatma Gandhi went to Ahmedabad to organise a satyagraha movement amongst whom?
o: Indigo planters
Cotton mill workers
Tea plantation workers
Railway porters
e: In 1918, Mahatma Gandhi went to Ahmedabad to organise a satyagraha movement amongst cotton mill workers.

q: When did Mahatma Gandhi lead a satyagraha to support the peasants of the Kheda district of Gujarat?
e: In 1917, Gandhiji organised a satyagraha to support the peasants of Kheda district in Gujarat, who could not pay revenue due to crop failure and a plague epidemic.

q: What was the motto/slogan raised by Gandhiji in his famous 8 August 1942 speech during the Quit India Movement?
o: Swaraj is my birthright
Do or Die (करो या मरो)
Jai Hind
Simon Go Back
e: On 8 August 1942 in Bombay, Gandhiji delivered the famous "Do or Die" speech calling for the orderly British withdrawal from India.

q: What name did Mahatma Gandhi give to the "untouchables" to assert their dignity?
o: Harijan (हरिजन)
Bahujan
Girmitiya
Swarajist
e: Mahatma Gandhi declared that swaraj would not come for a hundred years if untouchability was not eliminated, calling the untouchables "harijan", or the children of God.

q: By how much did the import of foreign cloth drop between 1921 and 1922 during the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: From Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore (nearly halved)
From Rs 200 crore to Rs 180 crore
From Rs 50 crore to Rs 5 crore
It actually increased by 20%
e: As foreign cloth was boycotted and bonfires were lit, the import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.

q: Which party in Madras did NOT boycott the council elections during the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: Swaraj Party
Justice Party
Hindu Mahasabha
Muslim League
e: In Madras, the Justice Party — the party of the non-Brahmans — felt that entering the council was one way of gaining some power usually reserved only for Brahmans, so it did not boycott the elections.

q: Who set up the Oudh Kisan Sabha in October 1920 along with Baba Ramchandra and others?
o: Motilal Nehru
Jawaharlal Nehru
Sardar Patel
Subhas Chandra Bose
e: In June 1920 Jawaharlal Nehru toured Awadh villages, and by October 1920 the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra and a few others.

q: Which Act prohibited Assam plantation workers from leaving the tea gardens without permission?
o: Rowlatt Act of 1919
Inland Emigration Act of 1859
Forest Act of 1878
Criminal Tribes Act
e: Under the Inland Emigration Act of 1859, plantation workers in Assam were not permitted to leave the tea gardens without permission, and such permission was rarely granted.

q: What did the phrase "Gandhi Raj" mean to Assam tea garden workers when they left the plantations in 1921?
o: Higher tea export duties
Everyone would be given land in their own villages
Becoming managers of British companies
Moving permanently to Calcutta
e: Plantation workers interpreted swaraj in their own way: they left the plantations heading home believing Gandhi Raj was coming and everyone would be given land in their own villages.

q: Why was Alluri Sitaram Raju both respectful of Gandhi and yet convinced India could be liberated only by force?
o: He wore khadi and urged people to give up drinking, yet asserted India could be liberated only by the use of force, not non-violence
He supported British forest laws
He led the boycott in Bombay mills
He refused to help the tribal peasants
e: Raju talked of the greatness of Mahatma Gandhi, persuaded people to wear khadi and give up drinking, but at the same time asserted India could be liberated only by the use of force.

q: When was Alluri Sitaram Raju captured and executed by the British?
e: Raju was captured and executed in 1924, and over time became a folk hero among the tribal rebels of the Gudem Hills.

q: What was "Nai-dhobi bandhs" organised by panchayats in Awadh?
o: To ban Indian handloom cloth
To deprive landlords of the services of even barbers and washermen
To protest against Gandhiji's arrest
To collect funds for World War I
e: In many places in Awadh, nai-dhobi bandhs were organised by panchayats to deprive landlords of the services of even barbers and washermen as a form of social boycott.

q: According to the 1921 Census, roughly how many people perished in India due to famines and the influenza epidemic?
o: 1 to 2 million
12 to 13 million
50 million
5 lakh
e: According to the census of 1921, 12 to 13 million people perished as a result of famines and the influenza epidemic after World War I.

q: Who was the Viceroy who made a vague offer of "dominion status" for India in October 1929?
o: Lord Curzon
Lord Irwin
Lord Mountbatten
Lord Chelmsford
e: In an effort to win over Indian leaders, Viceroy Lord Irwin announced in October 1929 a vague offer of "dominion status" in an unspecified future and a Round Table Conference.

q: How many trusted volunteers accompanied Mahatma Gandhi on his 240-mile Dandi March?
e: Gandhiji started the Salt March on 12 March 1930 accompanied by 78 of his trusted volunteers, walking about 10 miles a day for 24 days over 240 miles.

q: Which rich peasant communities were most enthusiastic supporters of the Civil Disobedience Movement in the countryside?
o: Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh
Tenants of Bengal and Bihar
Planters of Assam
Fishermen of Kerala
e: Rich peasant communities like the Patidars of Gujarat and the Jats of Uttar Pradesh produced commercial crops and were hit hard by the Great Depression's falling prices and unable to pay revenue.

q: Which business federation was formed in 1927 to organise Indian business interests during the national movement?
o: East India Association
Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI)
Swaraj Party
All India Trade Union Congress
e: Indian merchants and industrialists formed the Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress in 1920 and the Federation of the Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industries (FICCI) in 1927.

q: Name two prominent industrialists who led the Indian business community in supporting the Civil Disobedience Movement initially.
o: Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla
Ratan Tata and Jamnalal Bajaj only
Lala Lajpat Rai and Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Nana Sahib and Tantia Tope
e: Led by prominent industrialists like Purshottamdas Thakurdas and G. D. Birla, the industrialists attacked colonial control over the Indian economy and gave financial assistance to CDM.

q: In 1930, thousands of workers in which Jharkhand/Chotanagpur mining area wore Gandhi caps and participated in protest rallies and boycott campaigns?
o: Jharia coal mines
Chotanagpur tin mines
Koderma mica mines
Singhbhum copper mines
e: NCERT specifically notes that in 1930 thousands of workers in Chotanagpur tin mines wore Gandhi caps and participated in protest rallies and boycott campaigns.

q: Why were industrial working classes generally absent in large numbers from the Civil Disobedience Movement (except in the Nagpur region)?
o: Because Congress banned workers completely
As industrialists came closer to the Congress, workers stayed aloof
Because workers supported the Simon Commission
Because all factories were closed in 1930
e: As the industrialists came closer to the Congress, workers stayed aloof because Congress was reluctant to include workers' demands as part of its programme of struggle.

q: In which year did the First World War begin and why did it create a new economic and political situation in India?
o: 1914; it led to huge defence expenditure financed by war loans and increasing taxes including customs duties and income tax
1919; it ended all taxes in India
1911; it brought cheaper European imports to India
1920; it immediately gave India Purna Swaraj
e: World War I (1914–1918) caused a huge increase in British defence expenditure; customs duties were raised and income tax introduced, while prices doubled between 1913 and 1918.

q: Where was the Non-Cooperation compromise finally worked out in December 1920 after initial debate at Calcutta in September 1920?
o: Lahore
Nagpur
Surat
Karachi
e: At the Calcutta session in September 1920, Gandhi convinced leaders of the need for NCM, and finally at the Nagpur session in December 1920 a compromise was worked out.

q: Who designed the Swadeshi tricolour flag during the Swadeshi movement in Bengal?
o: It had eight lotuses representing eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon representing Hindus and Muslims
It had a spinning wheel in the centre and was white, green and red
It had Ashoka Chakra with 24 spokes
It had only plain saffron cloth
e: During the Swadeshi movement in Bengal, a tricolour flag (red, green and yellow) was designed with eight lotuses representing eight provinces of British India and a crescent moon representing Hindus and Muslims.

q: Why did Dr B. R. Ambedkar clash with Mahatma Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference in 1931?
o: Salt tax abolition
Demand for separate electorates for Dalits
Participation in World War II
Formation of FICCI
e: Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits at the Second Round Table Conference, which Gandhi opposed because he feared it would slow down their integration into society.

q: What happened during the April 1930 protest in Sholapur after Gandhiji was arrested?
o: Only students stayed home silently
Industrial workers attacked police posts, municipal buildings, lawcourts and railway stations—all structures symbolising British rule
Businessmen closed banks permanently
General Dyer imposed martial law in Gujarat
e: A month after Abdul Ghaffar Khan's arrest, when Mahatma Gandhi himself was arrested, industrial workers in Sholapur attacked police posts, municipal buildings, lawcourts and railway stations.

q: Why did the Non-Cooperation Movement in cities gradually slow down?
o: Khadi cloth was often more expensive than mass-produced mill cloth, and alternative Indian institutions were slow to come up
British government lowered all taxes to zero
Gandhiji ordered students back to British schools in 1921
All lawyers stopped practising permanently
e: Poor people could not afford to buy expensive khadi for long, and because alternative Indian schools and courts were slow to develop, students and teachers began trickling back to government schools and lawyers joined back in courts.

q: Who presided over the historic Lahore Congress session in December 1929?
o: Motilal Nehru
Jawaharlal Nehru
Mahatma Gandhi
C. R. Das
e: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the December 1929 Lahore session of the Indian National Congress where Purna Swaraj was declared.

q: On 31 January 1930, Mahatma Gandhi sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating how many demands, and which one was the most stirring of all?
o: Five demands; abolition of Simon Commission
Eleven demands; abolition of the salt tax
Fourteen demands; separate electorates
Twenty demands; end of zamindari
e: On 31 January 1930, Gandhiji sent a letter to Viceroy Irwin stating eleven demands wide-ranging enough to stir all classes; the most stirring of all was the demand to abolish the salt tax.

q: Who was the Hindu Mahasabha leader who strongly opposed Jinnah's compromise proposal on Muslim representation at the All Parties Conference in 1928?
o: Madan Mohan Malaviya
M. R. Jayakar
Lala Lajpat Rai
V. D. Savarkar
e: At the All Parties Conference in 1928, all hope of resolving the issue over reserved seats in the Central Assembly disappeared when M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed efforts at compromise.

q: Who wrote an emotional letter to the British Indian history textbooks/colonial accounts? No — which Indian leader died after being assaulted by police during a demonstration against the Simon Commission in 1928?
o: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
Lala Lajpat Rai
Bipin Chandra Pal
Gopal Krishna Gokhale
e: Lala Lajpat Rai was assaulted by the British police during a peaceful demonstration against the Simon Commission in Lahore in 1928 and succumbed to injuries.

q: When was the Rowlatt Satyagraha launched with a nationwide hartal?
o: 6 April 1919
13 April 1919
10 April 1919
1 August 1920
e: Mahatma Gandhi wanted non-violent civil disobedience against such unjust laws as the Rowlatt Act, which was started with a hartal on 6 April 1919.

q: In 1928, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel led a successful peasant satyagraha against enhancement of land revenue in which taluka of Gujarat?
o: Kheda
Bardoli
Champaran
Anand
e: In 1928, Vallabhbhai Patel led the peasant movement in Bardoli, a taluka in Gujarat, against enhancement of land revenue, known as the Bardoli Satyagraha (Box in NCERT).

q: How did the Congress respond to the "No-Rent" campaign of poorer peasants during the Civil Disobedience Movement?
o: Congress wholeheartedly supported it everywhere
Apprehensive of raising issues that might upset the rich peasants and landlords, Congress was unwilling to support "no rent" campaigns
Congress made it mandatory for all provinces
Congress arrested the peasants itself
e: Poorer peasants wanted unpaid rent to landlords remitted, often joining radical socialist/communist movements; apprehensive of upsetting rich peasants and landlords, Congress was unwilling to support "no rent" campaigns.

q: What was "Satyagraha" according to Mahatma Gandhi?
o: Physical vengeance against the oppressor
The power of truth and the need to search for truth through non-violence, appealing to the conscience of the oppressor
Complete refusal to communicate with any ruler
Secret guerrilla warfare in forests
e: Gandhiji explained that Satyagraha is not physical force; a satyagrahi does not inflict pain on the adversary, seeking instead to win the battle through non-violence by appealing to the oppressor's conscience.

q:
Arrange the following events of the Indian National Movement in chronological order:
I. Chauri Chaura incident
II. Jallianwala Bagh massacre
III. Dandi March
IV. Poona Pact
o: II → I → III → IV
I → II → III → IV
II → III → I → IV
III → II → I → IV
e: Jallianwala Bagh (April 1919) → Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922) → Dandi March (March–April 1930) → Poona Pact (September 1932).

q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi see "Salt" as a powerful symbol that could unite the nation in 1930?
o: Salt was used only by industrialists in cities
Salt was an essential item of food consumed by the rich and poor alike, so the salt tax and British monopoly revealed the most oppressive face of British rule
Salt could only be imported from England
Salt was mainly used in industrial machinery
e: Salt was something consumed by the rich and the poor alike, and it was one of the most essential items of food; thus tax on salt and government monopoly over its production showed the most oppressive face of colonial rule.

q: How did the Civil Disobedience Movement differ fundamentally from the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: Civil Disobedience rejected non-violence completely
In Non-Cooperation people were asked to refuse cooperation with the British; in Civil Disobedience people were also asked to actively break colonial laws
Non-Cooperation allowed foreign cloth while CDM banned khadi
Civil Disobedience had no participation from women
e: During the Civil Disobedience Movement, people were asked not only to refuse cooperation with the British (as in 1921–22) but also to break colonial laws such as the salt law and forest laws.

q: Why did General Dyer later state that he opened fire at Jallianwala Bagh without warning to "produce a moral effect"?
o: He wanted to create in the minds of satyagrahis a feeling of terror and awe
He mistook the Baisakhi crowd for an invading foreign army
He wanted to help Baba Ramchandra in Awadh
He was obeying an order from the Congress
e: Dyer later declared his object was to "produce a moral effect", to create in the minds of satyagrahis a feeling of terror and awe.

q: What was the main reason Mahatma Gandhi decided to join forces with the Khilafat issue in 1919–1920?
o: To abolish all elections in Britain
He saw it as a golden opportunity to bring Hindus and Muslims together under the umbrella of a unified national movement
Because the British asked him to support the Ottoman Empire
Because he wanted to travel to Turkey
e: Gandhiji saw the Rowlatt Satyagraha's limitation (mostly confined to cities and towns) and realised that no broad-based movement could be organised without bringing Hindus and Muslims closer together via Khilafat.

q: Why were many Congress leaders reluctant to accept Gandhiji's Non-Cooperation proposal initially in September 1920?
o: They did not want to boycott the council elections scheduled for November 1920 and feared the movement might lead to popular violence
They wanted immediate war with Japan
They supported the Rowlatt Act
They felt taxes were too low
e: Many Congress members were reluctant to boycott the November 1920 council elections and feared the movement might trigger popular violence before a compromise was reached at Nagpur in December 1920.

q: Why did the tribal peasants of the Gudem Hills turn to guerrilla rebellion under Alluri Sitaram Raju?
o: The colonial government closed large forest areas, preventing them from grazing cattle or collecting fuelwood and fruits, and forced them to contribute unpaid begar for road building
Because the British gave them too much fertile land
Because landlords lowered their rents
Because they wanted separate electorates in London
e: Colonial forest restrictions hit both their livelihoods and traditional rights, and when the government forced them to contribute begar for road building, the hill people revolted.

q: How did the Great Depression of 1929 affect India's countryside and create conditions for the Civil Disobedience Movement?
o: Agricultural prices doubled and farmers became wealthy
Agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after 1930, making peasants unable to sell harvests and pay revenue
Exports surged tenfold
Revenue demands were completely abolished by Britain
e: As agricultural prices collapsed after 1930 and the colonial government refused to reduce revenue demands, peasants found it impossible to pay taxes, fuelling widespread rural unrest.

q: What was the primary demand of Indian industrialists when they supported the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930?
o: Protection against imports of foreign goods and a rupee-sterling foreign exchange ratio that would discourage imports
Total abolition of all private factories
Higher import taxes on Indian cotton goods in India
Immediate nationalisation of FICCI
e: Industrialists wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a favourable rupee-sterling foreign exchange ratio that would discourage imports and protect Indian industry.

q: Why did Indian business groups become less enthusiastic when the Civil Disobedience Movement was relaunched after the Second Round Table Conference?
o: They were apprehensive of the spread of militant activities, worried about prolonged disruption of business, and feared the growing influence of socialism amongst younger Congress members
British goods vanished from Indian markets permanently
FICCI was banned by Gandhi
All British factories were handed over to them
e: After the failure of the Second Round Table Conference, business groups were no longer uniformly enthusiastic; they feared prolonged business disruption and the growing influence of socialism in Congress.

q: How did the reinterpretation of history help create a feeling of nationalism in India by the end of the 19th century?
o: Indians began writing about glorious achievements in ancient India (art, architecture, science, mathematics, religion, philosophy) before colonial decline
British writers praised Indian industrial supremacy after 1857
Indians stopped reading all historical texts
Historians claimed India had no history before 1757
e: In response to British portrayal of Indians as backward and primitive, Indian writers looked into the past to discover great achievements in art, science, mathematics, religion and trade, urging readers to take pride and fight colonial decline.

q: What was a notable limitation in the participation of women during the Gandhian nationalist movements?
o: Gandhiji remained convinced it was the duty of women to look after home and hearth, and for a long time Congress was reluctant to allow women to hold any position of authority within the organisation
Women were barred from participating in salt manufacturing
Only rural illiterate women joined picketing
Women were not allowed to wear khadi
e: Even though women came out in thousands to picket liquor shops and make salt, Gandhiji felt their primary duty was looking after home and hearth, and Congress was long reluctant to give them positions of authority, seeking mainly their symbolic presence.

q: Why did many Muslim political organisations show a lukewarm response to the Civil Disobedience Movement after the decline of the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat movement?
o: A large section of Muslims felt alienated from Congress as from the mid-1920s Congress came to be more visibly associated with openly Hindu religious nationalist groups like the Hindu Mahasabha
Muslims completely supported the British Salt Tax
Khilafat Committee banned Muslims from salt making
Congress had merged with the Muslim League in 1925
e: After the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat movement ended, Congress appeared visibly closer to Hindu Mahasabha; worsening Hindu-Muslim relations and clashes over reserved seats in the Central Assembly (1928) created an atmosphere of suspicion.

q: What was Muhammad Ali Jinnah's key condition in 1927 for giving up the demand for separate Muslim electorates?
o: Guaranteed reserved seats in the Central Assembly and representation in proportion to population in Muslim-dominated provinces (Bengal and Punjab)
Partition of India in 1928
Immediate departure of the Simon Commission to Turkey
Replacing Hindi with Persian
e: Jinnah was willing to give up the demand for separate electorates if Muslims were assured reserved seats in the Central Assembly and representation in proportion to population in Bengal and Punjab.

q: Identify the mistake in how Awadh peasants carried out the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1921, which worried the Congress leadership:
o: Houses of talukdars and merchants were attacked, bazaars were looted, grain hoards were taken over, and local leaders invoked Gandhi's name saying no taxes were to be paid
Peasants paid double taxes voluntarily
Peasants refused to join Oudh Kisan Sabha
Peasants built new railways for the British
e: As the movement spread in 1921, talukdars' houses were attacked and bazaars looted; local leaders even told peasants Gandhiji had declared land was to be redistributed among the poor, causing Congress leadership concern.

q: How did industrial workers express selective solidarity in Nagpur and elsewhere during the Civil Disobedience Movement?
o: Some workers selectively adopted Gandhian boycott of foreign goods as part of their own struggle against low wages and poor working conditions, e.g., railway workers (1930), dockworkers (1932), and Chotanagpur tin mine workers (1930)
They boycotted all Indian-owned mills
They supported the Simon Commission in Nagpur
They worked only in Calcutta jute mills without strikes
e: Despite staying mostly aloof because of Congress's closeness to industrialists, railway workers struck in 1930, dockworkers in 1932, and thousands in Chotanagpur tin mines wore Gandhi caps in 1930.

It recommended immediate partition of Bengal
It increased the salt tax to 500%
It appointed Gandhi as Viceroy without consulting Nehru
e: Constituted under Sir John Simon in 1927 by the Tory government in Britain, the commission had not a single Indian member, sparking unified "Go back Simon" protests upon arriving in 1928.

q:

o: (i)-Awadh peasants, (ii)-Gudem Hills guerrilla struggle, (iii)-Swaraj Party, (iv)-Tamil folk tales

(i)-Gudem Hills, (ii)-Tamil folk tales, (iii)-Awadh peasants, (iv)-Swaraj Party
(i)-Tamil folk tales, (ii)-Swaraj Party, (iii)-Gudem Hills, (iv)-Awadh peasants
e: Baba Ramchandra led Awadh peasants; Alluri Sitaram Raju led Gudem Hills tribal rebels; C. R. Das co-founded Swaraj Party; Natesa Sastri published The Folklore of Southern India.

q: What did Rabindranath Tagore do in Bengal as part of the movement to revive Indian folklore?
o: He personally began collecting ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, and led the movement for folk revival
He banned Bengali folk songs
He painted the 1905 Bharat Mata image instead of Abanindranath
He founded the Justice Party
e: In Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore himself began collecting ballads, nursery rhymes and myths, and led the movement for folk revival.

q: In Gandhi's view (in Hind Swaraj, 1909), how would British rule in India collapse within a year?
o: If Indians refused to cooperate with the British, Swaraj would come within a year
If Indian princes attacked London
If all rivers dried up
If Britain surrendered to the Ottoman Empire

q: What was the main objective of the Poona Pact (September 1932) regarding the "Depressed Classes"?
o: Reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils, to be voted in by the general electorate
Separate independent country for Dalits
Separate electorates where only Dalits voted
Abolition of all elections in India

q: Which stages did Gandhiji propose for unfolding the Non-Cooperation Movement?
o: First surrender of government titles; then boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, legislative councils, schools and foreign goods; and if the government used repression, launch a full civil disobedience campaign
Immediate violent capture of Delhi without any boycott
First close all Indian mills, then surrender titles
First abolish all panchayats, then pay higher taxes
e: Gandhiji proposed that the movement unfold in stages: surrender of titles awarded by government, boycott of civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods, followed by full civil disobedience if repressed.

q: Which image of Bharat Mata contrasting Abanindranath Tagore's 1905 painting later circulated in popular prints?
o: Holding a trishul, standing beside a lion and an elephant — symbols of power and authority
Wearing only British military uniform
Sitting inside a London factory
Holding the Union Jack
e: In subsequent years, the image of Bharat Mata acquired many different forms in popular prints, including one showing her with a trishul, standing beside a lion and an elephant—both symbols of power and authority.

q: What happened to the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1934 after Gandhiji relaunched it in 1932?
o: It continued with doubled momentum in 1934
It lost its momentum by 1934
It immediately achieved Purna Swaraj in 1934
It merged into the Khilafat Movement in 1934
e: After returning disappointed from the Second Round Table Conference (Dec 1931), Gandhiji found Congress declared illegal and leaders jailed; he relaunched CDM, which continued for over a year but by 1934 lost its momentum.

q: During the Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh protests in Punjab, how did the colonial government respond?
o: Immediate withdrawal of the Rowlatt Act

Granted independence to Punjab
Appointed Indian judges to every court
e: Seeing violence spread after 13 April 1919, the government responded with brutal repression seeking to humiliate and terrorise people, even bombing villages around Gujranwala in Punjab (now in Pakistan).

q: In 1920, what role did Mahatma Gandhi and Shaukat Ali undertake across India?
o: They toured extensively to mobilise popular support for the Non-Cooperation–Khilafat Movement
They travelled to London to sign the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
They led the Dandi Salt March
They formed the Swaraj Party
e: Throughout the summer of 1920 Mahatma Gandhi and Shaukat Ali toured extensively across India, mobilising popular support for the combined Non-Cooperation–Khilafat movement.

q: What was "forced recruitment" carried out by the British in Indian villages during World War I?
o: A process by which the colonial state forced people in rural areas to join the British Indian army
Hiring village teachers forcefully
Mandatory plantation labour in Champaran
Compulsory voting in council elections

q: Which regions saw dramatic participation of women during the Salt Satyagraha and Civil Disobedience Movement?
o: In urban areas mostly from high-caste families; in rural areas mostly from rich peasant households
Only European women living in Calcutta
Only royal queens from princely states
Only factory managers from London
e: During CDM, thousands of women came out of their homes to listen to Gandhiji, manufacture salt, picket foreign cloth and liquor shops; in urban areas they were mainly from high-caste families and in rural areas from rich peasant households.

q: Why was the Congress Working Committee meeting at Wardha on 14 July 1942 significant?
o: It passed the historic Quit India resolution demanding immediate transfer of power to Indians and withdrawal of the British
It called off the Civil Disobedience Movement
It welcomed the Simon Commission
It signed the Lucknow Pact
e: The Congress Working Committee in its meeting in Wardha on 14 July 1942 passed the historic Quit India resolution, later endorsed by the AICC in Bombay on 8 August 1942.

q: How did the plantation workers in Assam misunderstand the Swaraj call in 1921, and what happened to them on their way home?
o: Defying authorities, thousands left plantations believing Gandhi Raj was coming, but stranded by a railway and steamer strike, they were caught by police and brutally beaten up
They reached Bihar safely in British trains
They were gifted tea estates by the British
They joined the Justice Party in Madras
e: Defying authorities, plantation workers left tea gardens heading home, but because of a railway and steamer strike they were stranded on the way, caught by police and brutally beaten up.

(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) directly explains Gandhiji's strategic integration of the Khilafat committee into Non-Cooperation.

Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.

Assertion (A): The Congress leadership was completely happy with the violent tactics used by peasants in Awadh in 1921.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

q:
Assertion (A): Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and the Chauri Chaura incident directly caused Gandhiji to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement.

q:
Assertion (A): Within the Congress, younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for more radical mass agitation and for full independence.
Reason (R): C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true historical facts about internal debates inside the Congress in the 1920s, but (R) is a parallel development rather than the cause of (A).

q:
Assertion (A): When the Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928, it was welcomed with garlands by the Congress and Muslim League.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) explains why Gandhiji chose salt to launch the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930.

q:
Assertion (A): Rich peasant communities like the Patidars of Gujarat and Jats of Uttar Pradesh were active in the Civil Disobedience Movement.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) explains why rich peasants joined CDM enthusiastically as a struggle against high revenues.

Assertion (A): Rich peasants remained deeply disappointed when the Civil Disobedience Movement was called off in 1931 without the revenue rates being revised.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: (A) is true, but (R) is false because when the movement was restarted in 1932, many of those disappointed rich peasants REFUSED to participate.

Assertion (A): Congress was eager to support the "no rent" campaigns of the poorer peasants during the Civil Disobedience Movement.
Reason (R): The Congress did not want to upset the rich peasants and landlords.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.

Assertion (A): Dr B. R. Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for Dalits at the Second Round Table Conference.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Assertion (A): The Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

Reason (R): Images of Bharat Mata helped people identify with the nation through devotion to this mother figure.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is true, but (R) is false.

Assertion (A): In 1921, Gandhiji designed a Swaraj flag with red, green and yellow colours and eight lotuses.

o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

q:
Assertion (A): During the Civil Disobedience Movement, Congress never allowed women to participate in picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops.
Reason (R): Many women went to jail during the movement as they began to see service to the nation as a sacred duty.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

(A) is true, but (R) is false.
(A) is false, but (R) is true.
e: (A) is false because women participated actively in picketing foreign cloth and liquor shops, salt manufacture and protest marches. (R) is true.

q: Case Study: "On 13 April the infamous Jallianwalla Bagh incident took place. On that day a large crowd gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwalla Bagh. Because newspapers banned all fairs
Because Gandhiji lifted martial law on 12 April
Because the fair was held in Lahore
e: Being from outside the city, many villagers were unaware of the martial law that had been imposed in Amritsar by General Dyer.

q: Case Study: "General Dyer entered the area, blocked the exit points, and opened fire on the crowd, killing hundreds." Which immediate reaction broke out across north Indian towns after news of Jallianwala Bagh spread?
o: Strikes, clashes with the police and attacks on government buildings broke out in many north Indian towns
Complete silence and cooperation with Dyer
Immediate end of World War I
Peasants paid double revenue voluntarily
e: As the news of Jallianwala Bagh spread, crowds took to the streets in many north Indian towns with strikes, police clashes and attacks on government buildings.

q: Case Study: "While the Rowlatt satyagraha had been a widespread movement, it was still limited mostly to cities and towns. Mahatma Gandhi now felt the need to launch a more broad-based movement in India." Why did Gandhiji choose the Khilafat issue to broaden the movement?
o: He saw this as an opportunity to bring Muslims under the umbrella of a unified national movement alongside Hindus
He wanted to abolish the Congress party
He supported British control over Ottoman territories
To prevent rural peasants from joining
e: Gandhiji knew no broad-based movement could succeed without Hindu-Muslim unity, so at the Calcutta session in September 1920 he convinced other leaders to start NCM in support of Khilafat as well as swaraj.

q: Case Study: "What was Gandhiji's central argument in Hind Swaraj (1909) justifying non-cooperation?"
o: British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived only because of this cooperation
British rule was maintained solely through industrial railways
Indians could overthrow the British only by forming European alliances
Foreign cloth was superior to khadi
e: In Hind Swaraj (1909), Gandhiji argued that if Indians refused to cooperate, British rule in India would collapse within a year and swaraj would come.

q: Case Study: "Within the Congress, C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru were tired of mass struggles and wanted to participate in elections to the provincial councils set up by the Government of India Act of 1919." What argument did they give for forming the Swaraj Party?
o: To oppose British policies within the councils, argue for reform and demonstrate that these councils were not truly democratic
To merge Congress permanently with the British Tory party
To support the Simon Commission
To boycott the 1929 Lahore resolution
e: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru felt it was important to oppose British policies within the councils, argue for reform and also demonstrate that these councils were not truly democratic.

q: Case Study: "Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation, when they discover some unity that binds them together. History and fiction, folklore and songs, popular prints and symbols, all played a part in the making of nationalism." Which figure painted by Abanindranath Tagore in 1905 first gave a visual identity to India?
o: Bharat Mata depicted as an ascetic figure dispensing learning, food and clothing
Marianne wearing a red cap
General Dyer in Amritsar
Bankim Chandra holding a spinning wheel
e: Abanindranath Tagore painted Bharat Mata in 1905 as an ascetic figure — calm, composed, divine and spiritual — with a mala in one hand.

q: Case Study: "Why did nationalists in the late nineteenth century begin recording folk tales sung by bards and touring villages to gather folk songs and legends?"
o: They believed these tales gave a true picture of traditional culture that had been corrupted and damaged by outside forces, helping discover national identity and restore pride in one's past
To submit tax records to the British Viceroy
To teach English grammar in London
To promote British mill cloth in villages
e: Nationalists believed preserving folk tradition was essential to discover one's national identity and restore a sense of pride in one's past.

q: Case Study: "How did the reinterpretation of history sometimes create problems in unifying all Indians?"
o: When the past being glorified was Hindu and images celebrated were drawn from Hindu iconography, people of other communities felt left out
Nobody read historical books in the 19th century
Only British authors wrote nationalist histories
Folklore was completely banned in Madras
e: NCERT notes that these efforts to unify people were not without problems: when the past being glorified was Hindu and images drawn from Hindu iconography, people of other communities felt left out.

q: Case Study: "For long the Congress had ignored the dalits, for fear of offending the sanatanis, the conservative high-caste Hindus." Why did Mahatma Gandhi take a different stand on untouchability?
o: Gandhiji declared that swaraj would not come for a hundred years if untouchability was not eliminated, organised satyagraha to secure their entry into temples and public wells, and personally cleaned toilets to dignify bhangi work
Gandhiji demanded that Dalits leave India
Gandhiji banned Dalits from entering Congress meetings
Gandhiji supported separate electorates at the RTC
e: Mahatma Gandhi called untouchables "harijan", organised satyagraha for their access to temples, public wells, tanks, roads and schools, and persuaded upper castes to change their heart.

q: Case Study: "Even after the Poona Pact of September 1932 gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats in legislative councils, how did the dalit movement still view the Congress-led national movement?"
o: The dalit movement continued to be apprehensive of the Congress-led national movement and many leaders still felt political empowerment would solve their social disabilities
Every Dalit immediately joined the Hindu Mahasabha
Dalits boycotted all future elections forever
Ambedkar resigned from politics in 1932
e: Despite the Poona Pact, the dalit movement continued to be apprehensive of the Congress-led national movement, and dalit participation remained limited particularly in the Maharashtra and Nagpur region where their organisation was quite strong.

q:

q: Why was Dr Ambedkar's organisation in Maharashtra and the Nagpur region particularly influential during the 1930s, limiting Dalit participation in the Civil Disobedience Movement there?
o: Because Dalit organisation (Depressed Classes Association) was quite strong there and many Dalit leaders believed political empowerment through separate electorates, not Gandhian Congress-led movement, would resolve their social disabilities
Because Salt March never passed near Maharashtra
Because General Dyer banned meetings in Nagpur in 1930
Because industrialists in Nagpur paid the highest wages in India
e: NCERT notes that Dalit participation in CDM was limited, particularly in Maharashtra and Nagpur region where their organisation was quite strong and leaders demanded reserved seats and separate electorates.

q: Compare the Non-Cooperation peasant movement in Awadh with the tribal movement in the Gudem Hills. Which similarity existed between them?
o: Both saw local leaders reinterpret Gandhian/Swaraj ideals in ways that went beyond Congress's strict non-violent programme
Both were led directly by Mahatma Gandhi in person
Both strictly prohibited any attack on landlords or police
Both began after the Poona Pact of 1932
e: In Awadh, peasants attacked talukdars' mansions and looted bazaars invoking Gandhi's name; in Gudem Hills, Alluri Sitaram Raju admired Gandhi and khadi yet waged armed guerrilla warfare against police stations.

q: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched regarding early Gandhian satyagrahas in India?
o: Champaran (1917) — Bihar indigo peasants against oppressive plantation system
Kheda (1917) — Gujarat peasants demanding revenue relaxation due to crop failure and plague
Ahmedabad (1918) — Cotton mill workers satyagraha
Bardoli (1919) — Led by Mahatma Gandhi against the Rowlatt Act
e: The fourth pair is incorrect: the Bardoli Satyagraha took place in 1928 (not 1919) and was led by Vallabhbhai Patel (not Gandhi against Rowlatt Act) against enhancement of land revenue.

q: Why did many Indian industrialists initially view the Gandhian boycott positively yet grow anxious during prolonged strikes?
o: Initially they saw swaraj as freedom from colonial restrictions on trade and industry, but later feared militant disruption of business and the spread of socialism
Because British goods stopped selling completely in 1930
Because Congress demanded the immediate closure of all Indian textile mills
Because they lost FICCI leadership to the British
e: Business classes supported CDM in 1930 hoping colonial business restrictions would end, but after the failed 2nd RTC they worried about militant strikes, business disruption and socialism among younger Congress leaders.

3. All Parties Conference in 1928 solved the problem permanently.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true. Statement 3 is false because all hope of resolving the issue at the 1928 All Parties Conference disappeared when M. R. Jayakar of the Hindu Mahasabha strongly opposed compromise.

q: Why was Sir Muhammad Iqbal's 1930 Muslim League presidential address politically important?
o: He reiterated the importance of separate electorates for Muslims as an important safeguard for their minority political interests, which critics later saw as intellectual justification for Pakistan
He demanded the abolition of all reserved seats
He merged the Muslim League into the Justice Party
He joined the Dandi March in Gujarat
e: In 1930, Sir Muhammad Iqbal, as President of the Muslim League, reiterated the importance of separate electorates for Muslims as a safeguard for their minority political interests (NCERT Source D).

q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi undertake a fast unto death in September 1932?
o: Because the British government conceded Dr Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates for Dalits, which Gandhi feared would slow down their integration into society
To protest against the Quit India resolution
To demand the partition of Bengal
To support the Rowlatt Act
e: When the British government conceded Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates for Dalits, Gandhiji began a fast unto death, believing separate electorates would hamper their social integration; this led to the Poona Pact.

q: What was the significance of the Lahore Independence Day Pledge taken on 26 January 1930?
o: It declared Indians' inalienable right to freedom and complete Swaraj, though celebrations attracted very little attention, prompting Gandhi to relate freedom to concrete everyday issues like Salt
It brought immediate British withdrawal in January 1930
It launched the Quit India Movement
It was signed only by the Justice Party
e: The 26 January 1930 celebrations attracted very little attention, so Mahatma Gandhi had to find a way to relate this abstract idea of freedom to more concrete issues of everyday life — leading to his Salt March letter.

q: How did the production of Indian textile mills and handlooms benefit during the Non-Cooperation Movement (1921–22)?
o: As people began discarding imported clothes and wearing only Indian ones, production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up
Indian mills shut down due to khadi boycott
Imported British cloth doubled in value
Cotton cultivation stopped in Gujarat
e: With foreign goods boycotted, liquor shops picketed and foreign cloth burnt in huge bonfires, people discarded imported clothes and wore Indian cloth, causing Indian mill and handloom production to rise.

q: Which leader's speech in 1921 near Rae Bareli had Congress volunteers preventing peasants from confronting police, inspiring Nehru's reflection on Gandhian restraint?
o: When police fired at peasants near Rae Bareli on 6 January 1921, Nehru felt agitated and angry, yet calmed himself thinking of Gandhiji's non-violence and admired the peaceful peasants
Nehru ordered peasants to attack Allahabad police station
Nehru resigned from Congress immediately
Nehru joined the British army
e: In Source B (Sarvapalli Gopal's biography of Nehru), on 6 January 1921 near Rae Bareli, Nehru was stopped from going to the site of police firing; initially angry, the moment passed as he remembered Gandhiji's message of non-violence.

q: What was "Satyagraha" compared to "passive resistance" according to Mahatma Gandhi (NCERT Source A)?
o: Passive resistance is considered the weapon of the weak, whereas Satyagraha is pure soul-force requiring intense activity and truth without ill-will against the adversary
Both are identical armed rebellions
Satyagraha encourages burning enemies while passive resistance does not
Passive resistance was invented in Champaran
e: In Source A, Gandhiji explains that passive resistance is misconstrued as a weapon of the weak, whereas the power of satyagraha is not physical force—it is pure soul-force where truth and love are its substance.

q: What happened during the Non-Cooperation Movement in cities across provinces regarding council elections, lawyers and students?
o: Thousands of students left government-controlled schools/colleges, headmasters and teachers resigned, lawyers gave up legal practices, and council elections were boycotted in most provinces except Madras
All elections were won by the British Labour Party
Every province except Bombay participated fully in council elections
Only doctors went on strike while students stayed in government schools
e: Middle-class participation in cities saw massive resignations by teachers, boycott by students and lawyers, and council election boycotts in all provinces except Madras (where the Justice Party contested).

q: Why was the Chauri Chaura incident (1922) a turning point for the Congress strategy in the 1920s?
o: It led Gandhiji to withdraw NCM because satyagrahis needed proper training before mass struggles, shifting focus towards constructive work and council debates (Swaraj Party)
It caused an immediate war between India and Britain
It convinced Gandhiji to form an armed guerrilla army
It ended all nationalist activity until 1942
e: Seeing NCM turning violent in many places and culminating at Chauri Chaura in February 1922, Gandhiji called it off, feeling satyagrahis needed to be properly trained before being ready for mass struggles.

q: Which statement accurately describes Mahatma Gandhi's action immediately after signing the Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931?
o: Gandhiji went to London in December 1931 for the Second Round Table Conference, but negotiations broke down and he returned disappointed to find repression renewed in India
India became independent in December 1931
Lord Irwin joined the Congress party
Abdul Ghaffar Khan presided over the London conference
e: In December 1931 Gandhiji went to London for the Second Round Table Conference, negotiations broke down, and upon returning he found Ghaffar Khan and Nehru in jail, Congress declared illegal, and boycotts banned.

q:
Read the three statements regarding Quit India Movement (1942):
1. Failure of the Cripps Mission and effects of WWII created widespread discontent in India.
2. At Bombay on 8 August 1942, the AICC endorsed the resolution for a non-violent mass struggle on the widest possible scale.
3. People observed hartals, demonstrations and processions with national songs and slogans.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
e: All three statements accurately summarise the Quit India Movement box in NCERT, including active participation by students, workers, peasants, leaders like Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali, Ram Manohar Lohia, and women like Matangini Hazra, Kanaklata Barua and Rama Devi.

q: Which woman freedom fighter mentioned in NCERT's Quit India Movement note became a martyr in Bengal/Assam/Odisha?
o: Matangini Hazra in Bengal, Kanaklata Barua in Assam and Rama Devi in Odisha
Queen Victoria, Sarojini Naidu and Annie Besant only
Madame Blavatsky and Margaret Noble
Louise Otto-Peters and Marianne
e: NCERT specifically notes women leaders in Quit India Movement: Matangini Hazra in Bengal, Kanaklata Barua in Assam, and Rama Devi in Odisha.

q: Why was Mahatma Gandhi alarmed by the 1919 Rowlatt Satyagraha violence and why did he still call it limited?
o: Because though widespread, it was confined mostly to cities and towns and had not yet unified rural masses and all religious communities on an all-India scale
Because only farmers in Assam participated
Because it lasted ten years
Because General Dyer supported it
e: Realising the Rowlatt Satyagraha was limited mostly to cities and towns, Gandhiji felt the need to launch a broader movement uniting Hindus and Muslims and spanning urban and rural India.

q: Which of the following correctly describes the Independence Day Pledge of 26 January 1930 (NCERT Source C)?
o: If any government deprives a people of their inalienable right to freedom and oppresses them, the people have a further right to alter it or to abolish it; the British government had ruined India economically, politically, culturally and spiritually
Indians must request only municipal council seats from Britain
Peasants must increase land revenue payments
India must never adopt Swadeshi cloth
e: The Independence Day Pledge (26 January 1930) declared that the British government in India not only deprived Indians of freedom but had based itself on exploitation and ruined India economically, politically, culturally and spiritually, so India must sever British connection and attain Purna Swaraj.

q: What did the "Oudh Kisan Sabha" accomplish within a month of its formation in October 1920?
o: Over 300 branches in villages around the region
Only 5 branches in Lucknow
1000 branches in Madras
12 branches in Champaran
e: Within a month of setting up the Oudh Kisan Sabha in October 1920, over 300 branches had been set up in the villages around the region, linking the peasant struggle to the wider Non-Cooperation Movement.

q: What demand did the peasants of Awadh raise under Baba Ramchandra's leadership?
o: Reduction of revenue, abolition of begar, and social boycott of oppressive landlords
Complete abolition of agriculture
Increase in forced labour on roads
Separate electorates for landlords
e: The Awadh peasant movement was against talukdars and landlords who demanded exorbitantly high rents and cesses; the peasant movement demanded reduction of revenue, abolition of begar, and social boycott of oppressive landlords.

q: Why was Dr Ambedkar willing to accept Gandhiji's position in the Poona Pact despite initially demanding separate electorates?
o: Because Gandhiji began a fast unto death fearing social division, and the compromise still guaranteed reserved seats in provincial and central legislative councils for the Depressed Classes
Because the British abolished all provincial councils
Because FICCI ordered Ambedkar to resign
Because separate electorates were banned by the Lahore session
e: When Gandhiji began a fast unto death against separate electorates, Ambedkar ultimately accepted Gandhiji's position to preserve social unity while securing reserved seats for Depressed Classes under the Poona Pact.

q: Which leader described the struggle in Bardoli (1928) or which leader from the North-West Frontier Province had angry crowds demonstrate in Peshawar streets on his arrest in April 1930?
o: Abdul Ghaffar Khan
Muhammad Ali Jinnah
Baba Ramchandra
Motilal Nehru
e: When Abdul Ghaffar Khan, a devout disciple of Mahatma Gandhi, was arrested in April 1930, angry crowds demonstrated in the streets of Peshawar, facing armoured cars and police firing.

q:
Look at the two Nationalist flags mentioned in NCERT:
(A) Swadeshi flag in Bengal (red, green, yellow)
(B) Gandhiji's 1921 Swaraj flag (red, green, white)
What replaced the eight lotuses and crescent moon in Gandhiji's 1921 flag?
o: A spinning wheel (charkha), representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help
An olive branch
A trident (trishul)
A lion and an elephant
e: Gandhiji's 1921 Swaraj flag retained red and green, substituted white for yellow, and placed a spinning wheel in the centre representing the Gandhian ideal of self-help.

q: Why was the First World War followed by acute food shortages in India in 1918–19 and 1920–21?
o: Crops failed in many parts of India, which combined with an influenza epidemic caused widespread starvation and 12–13 million deaths
Indian farmers stopped growing wheat voluntarily
The British destroyed all irrigation canals in 1918
All Indian grain was exported to China alone
e: In 1918–19 and 1920–21, crops failed in many parts of India, resulting in acute shortages of food, accompanied by a devastating influenza epidemic.

q: Which of the following correctly states the role of the Swaraj Party vs radical leaders in the mid-1920s?
o: C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru favoured fighting British policies inside provincial councils, whereas Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for radical mass agitation and full independence
Nehru and Bose founded the Justice Party in Madras
C. R. Das demanded immediate violent revolution in Gudem Hills
Both wings boycotted the 1929 Lahore session
e: The 1920s saw internal debates between Swarajists (C. R. Das, Motilal Nehru) wanting to enter councils and younger leaders (Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose) demanding full independence and radical mass struggle.

q: Why did the Civil Disobedience Movement invoke a different response from business classes compared to industrial workers?
o: Industrialists feared colonial restrictions on their businesses so they initially funded CDM, while workers stayed aloof because Congress grew close to industrialists and avoided workers' specific wage demands
Workers funded FICCI while industrialists went to jail in Sholapur
Both groups rejected Gandhiji from the start
Workers only supported British imports
e: Congress feared alienating industrialists and splitting anti-imperial forces if it included workers' demands, so industrial workers largely stayed aloof except in pockets like Nagpur and Chotanagpur.

q: Identify the TRUE pair of dates and events during the Salt Satyagraha (1930–1931):
o: 31 January 1930 (Letter of 11 demands) → 12 March 1930 (March begins) → 6 April 1930 (Salt law broken) → 5 March 1931 (Gandhi-Irwin Pact)
12 March 1930 (Gandhi-Irwin Pact) → 6 April 1930 (March begins) → 31 January 1931 (Salt law broken)
26 January 1930 (Salt law broken) → 12 March 1930 (Poona Pact)
6 April 1930 (Letter sent to Irwin) → 12 March 1930 (Second RTC)
e: This exact timeline—31 Jan 1930 ultimatum, 12 Mar 1930 Dandi March launch, 6 Apr 1930 Dandi salt law violation, and 5 Mar 1931 Gandhi-Irwin Pact—is directly documented in NCERT Chapter 2.

q: What was "Satyagraha" ultimately trying to appeal to in the British rulers, according to Mahatma Gandhi?
o: The oppressor's conscience — persuading them to see the truth rather than forcing them through violence
Their military ambition
Their desire to raise income taxes
Their loyalty to the Ottoman Empire
e: Gandhiji wrote that a satyagrahi appeals to the conscience of the oppressor so that people — including the oppressors — are persuaded to see the truth, instead of being forced to accept truth through violence.

q: Why was Mahatma Gandhi's 1920s Non-Cooperation call linked with "Swadeshi" and the "Spinning Wheel" (charkha)?
o: It symbolised economic self-help and indigenous production to replace imported British machine-made cloth, attacking British economic dominance while fostering national unity
It aimed to export khadi to Berlin
It banned Indian weavers from working in villages
It was required by the Inland Emigration Act
e: Rejecting foreign cloth for khadi and placing the spinning wheel at the centre of the 1921 Swaraj flag embodied the Gandhian ideal of self-help and struck directly at British commercial interests.
